title: Quartering and packing out game
def: Quartering means cutting a large animal into its four legs plus the backstraps, neck, and other meat so it can be carried out in loads and cooled faster.
look: clean game bags for each quarter
a sharp knife and a spare blade
a pack frame or sled for heavy loads
use: Skin one side at a time, take the front and hind quarters, backstraps, and tenderloins, bag each piece, and hang or lay the bags in shade to cool before carrying.
not: Do not leave meat in a pile on the ground in the sun, and check your state's evidence-of-sex and tagging rules before you separate parts.

title: Skinning and hanging a deer
def: Skinning removes the hide so meat can cool and stay clean; hanging lets the carcass cool and drain in cold, shaded, animal-proof conditions.
look: a stable gambrel or rope and a strong limb or beam
air at or below 40 °F (4 °C) for hanging
hair kept off the meat
use: Hang by the hind legs or the head, skin from the top down with the blade edge out, and keep the carcass cold and covered from flies and animals.
not: Do not hang meat in temperatures above 40 °F for long, and do not let pets or wildlife reach it.

title: Basic venison butchering cuts
def: Home butchering divides a deer into a few simple groups: backstraps and tenderloins for steaks, hind-quarter roasts, shoulder and neck for stew, and trim for grinding.
look: silver skin and fat trimmed off
a clean, cold work surface
meat wrapped airtight and labeled with date
use: Work cold and clean, trim fat, silver skin, and bloodshot meat, wrap tightly, label, and freeze.
not: Do not saw through bone or the spine in CWD areas, and do not leave meat warm on the counter while you work.

title: Tagging, transport, and checking in game
def: Most states require you to tag an animal right away, keep the tag with it during transport, and report or check in the harvest within a set time.
look: the tag filled out and attached as your state requires
the state's online, phone, or station check-in
rules on moving carcasses from CWD areas
use: Read your state agency's current tagging and check-in page before the season and follow it exactly.
not: Do not guess the deadline or carry an untagged animal; rules differ by state and change.

title: Using a processor when CWD is a concern
def: If you hunt where chronic wasting disease is found, ask a processor to process your animal by itself so its meat is not mixed with others.
look: the processor's policy on batch versus individual processing
test results before you eat the meat
how they dispose of bones and trimmings
use: Ask for individual processing, get the animal tested, and keep the meat frozen and unused until the result comes back.
not: Do not eat meat from an animal that tests positive.

title: Recovering game in water or thick cover
def: Getting an animal out of water, swamp, or thick cover comes after your own safety: cold water and deep mud can kill.
look: water depth, current, and temperature
ice that may not hold
dark or difficult ground near nightfall
use: Bring a partner and a rope, wait for light if needed, and reach the animal from shore or shallow water where you can.
not: Do not wade into deep, fast, or ice-cold water or walk onto thin ice for an animal.
call: Call 911 if anyone falls through ice or into cold water.

title: Ground blind safety
def: A ground blind hides you at ground level, but it also hides you from other hunters, so safe setup matters.
look: orange on the outside of the blind where required
a clear, safe shooting lane
a known exit route
use: Put orange on and around the blind as your state requires, know your shooting lanes and backstops, and keep the gun pointed out the window only when ready.
not: Do not run a heater with an open flame inside a closed blind; carbon monoxide builds fast.

title: Hunting with a young or new hunter
def: Mentoring a new or young hunter means close supervision, short trips, and teaching safety before success.
look: the new hunter within arm's reach when handling a gun
a completed hunter-education course where required
warm clothes, snacks, and a short plan
use: Keep sessions short and comfortable, review the firearm rules often, and check your state's youth and apprentice rules.
not: Do not hand an untrained person a loaded gun, or push a tired or cold child to stay out.

title: Black bear and moose around camps and carcasses
def: Black bears are drawn to carcasses, gut piles, and camp food, and a moose can charge if crowded, especially a cow with a calf or a bull in the rut.
look: fresh bear sign near a gut pile or meat pole
a moose with ears back and hackles raised
food or meat left out at camp
use: Hang meat away from sleeping areas, store food sealed, approach a kill carefully and make noise, and give moose plenty of room.
not: Do not approach a bear on a carcass or a moose at close range, and do not run from a bear.

title: Field dressing birds
def: Birds keep best when the crop and entrails are removed soon after the kill and the body is cooled.
look: gloves on
crop and intestines removed
the bird kept cool and dry
use: Remove the entrails and crop, wipe the cavity, and cool the bird quickly; pluck or skin at home.
not: Do not leave birds in a warm vest or pile them in a closed bag in warm weather.

title: Lead versus non-lead ammunition
def: Lead bullets can break into small fragments in meat, and scavengers such as eagles can be poisoned by lead in gut piles; non-lead options exist.
look: fragments spread several inches from the wound channel
federal non-toxic shot rules for waterfowl
local rules on lead ammunition
use: Trim generously around the wound channel, consider copper or other non-lead ammunition, and follow any rules where you hunt.
not: Do not feed trimmings from around a lead wound channel to children or pets.

title: Hunting ethics: no waste, respect for land and people
def: Ethical hunting means taking only shots you can make cleanly, using the animal well, and respecting landowners, other hunters, and the law.
look: permission in hand on private land
a plan to recover and use the meat
courtesy to others in the field
use: Practice before the season, pass on doubtful shots, recover and use what you take, and leave gates and land as you found them.
not: Do not waste meat, shoot from roads where it is illegal, or interfere with other hunters.

title: Land access, permission, and trespass
def: Hunting on private land needs the owner's permission, and posting and trespass rules differ from state to state; Yehsa has no property-owner map.
look: posted signs or paint marks on trees
a written or verbal permission you can show
public land boundaries on official maps
use: Ask permission early, carry the owner's contact, learn your state's posting rules, and check official public-land maps.
not: Do not cross onto land you are not sure about to follow game without permission.

title: Trapping is tightly regulated
def: Trapping usually needs its own license or education course and has strict rules on trap types, placement, checking times, and seasons.
look: the state's trapper-education requirement
trap check intervals
rules that protect pets and non-target animals
use: Take your state's trapper-education course and follow its current rules.
not: Yehsa does not give trap-setting instructions; do not set traps or snares without the license and training.

title: Game cameras: etiquette and privacy
def: Trail cameras record whatever passes, including people, so place them where you have permission and think about privacy.
look: the landowner's permission
trails used by hikers or neighbors
state rules on cameras during the season
use: Get permission, aim cameras at game trails rather than paths people use, and check whether your state limits cellular cameras.
not: Do not record people without consent where it is prohibited, or share images that show others.

title: Wind direction and your scent
def: Deer rely on smell, and your scent drifts downwind in a widening cone, so hunters set up with the wind blowing from the deer toward them.
look: wind direction from a light feather, milkweed fluff, or powder
thermals rising in the morning warmth and sinking in the evening
deer approaching from downwind
use: Check the wind before you walk in, approach and sit so the wind carries your scent away from where deer travel, and move if it shifts.
not: Do not walk your stand trail with the wind at your back toward the deer.

title: Dragging a deer without hurting yourself
def: Dragging a deer is hard work that strains the back and heart, especially in cold weather and for people who do not exercise.
look: chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness
a long or uphill drag
help available nearby
use: Use a sled or cart, get help, take frequent breaks, and quarter a large animal rather than drag it far.
not: Do not push through chest pain or breathlessness.
call: Call 911 for chest pain, pain spreading to the arm or jaw, or fainting.

title: Hunting alone: leave a plan
def: A solo hunter should leave a plan with someone: where you will park and sit, when you will be back, and when they should call for help.
look: a marked map or pin of your stand
a check-in time
a charged phone and a light
use: Leave the plan, carry a whistle, light, and first aid, and stick to your return time or update it.
not: Do not change areas without telling your contact.
call: Your contact should call 911 if you miss the agreed time and cannot be reached.
